newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina suspends sunseed price, warns exchange.
newsitem.headline: Argentina suspends sunseed price, warns exchange.

text.p: The Argentine government has suspended a regular quotation of off-floor Buenos Aires sunflower seed prices due to suspected price manipulation, Agriculture Secretariat Felipe Sola said Wednesday.
"Everyone in the market knows that there are purposeful gaps in information," used in determining the "camara arbitral" sunflower seed price for the port of Buenos Aires, Sola told a news conference.
The sunflower price previously quoted by the Buenos Aires "camara arbitral" will now be based on the Buenos Aires Futures Exchange spot price and will only be available on consultation, Sola said.
"The camara arbitral prices are obsolete and should gradually be replaced by the Buenos Aires Futures Exchange spot prices," he said.

Sola also warned the Buenos Aires Futures Exchange to speed its efforts to boost trading volume by reforms including trading at the same time as the Chicago Board of Trade. The government wants improvements in grain delivery procedures and a reduction in the number of traded months to seven.
"The Futures Exchange has to make itself more up to date, although it has resisted making itself up to date," he said.

The government's action on the sunflower seed price followed public complaints by the Confederation of Rural Associations of Buenos Aires and La Pampa (Carbap), a major farmers association, about "camaras arbitrales".
A large part of Argentina's large grain output is priced according to average off-floor trading values announced a day after trading by the groups known as "camaras arbitrales."

These "camera arbitral" prices are then used as the basis for a common grains sales contract known as "price to be fixed", under which grain is delivered but the price linked to the camaras arbitral price at a future date.
Carbap said it wants the law changed to allow "price to be fixed" contracts to be linked to the official Buenos Aires Futures Exchange prices.
It also called for the Futures Market to change its trading hours so that they coincide with those of the Chicago Board of Trade, which is the world leader in major products like soybeans.

This would mean ending the Futures Markets' current system of trading its four main products -- maize, wheat, soybeans, and sunflower seed -- in mini-sessions which come one after another and not simultaneously.
Only a small proportion of Argentina's 50-million tonne annual grain output is traded on the Futures Exchange.
